newsitem.title: USA: U.S. housing starts fall called a seasonal quirk.
newsitem.headline: U.S. housing starts fall called a seasonal quirk.

text.p: Despite a huge drop in U.S. housing starts in December, analysts said they still believe the economy grew at a healthy pace in the fourth quarter.
The Commerce Department reported housing starts slumped 12.2 percent last month after a revised 9.3 percent gain in November and a revised 5.2 percent fall in October.
Economists dismissed the latest data as a quirk in seasonal adjustment factors.
"This is the time of year when seasonals can wreak havoc on these numbers," said Mickey Levy, chief economist at NationsBanc Capital Markets.
"The number is negative, but I wouldn't read as much negativeness (as) the 12.2 percent decline suggests," Levy said. "I do not have the impression housing is going to tank."
Economists said the December housing starts figures should marginally lower fourth-quarter gross domestic product.

In addition to the seasonal adjustment problems, economists also pointed to the dismal weather on the West coast in December, where heavy rain caused flooding from the Pacific Northwest down to Northern California, as contributing to the starts decline.
Starts plunged 29.2 percent in the West, while starts in the rest of the country were down, but considerably less.
Starts in the Northeast fell 2.3 percent in December, and were down 7.2 percent in the South and 7.9 percent in the Midwest.
In addition, there were broad-based declines in most sectors, from single-family to multi-family housing.

"Any one month's number is dicey to read too much into," said Joseph Liro, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities, noting the up and down month-to-month pattern. "You have got to look at the trend."
Economists said the trend is for weakening housing activity in 1997, but not as dramatic as December's decline indicates.
Cheryl Katz, senior economist at Merrill Lynch & Co, noted that while starts rose 8.8 percent for all of 1996, starts were 5.3 percent lower in the fourth quarter than in the third quarter of 1996.
